verdicts.evidence: 'Why did Moon change its mind? What was the central message or lesson that Moon learned?' (Moon realized that the world is beautiful no matter if it's day or night, and Moon learned to appreciate his place in the night sky.)

clauses.clause: Apply knowledge of author, audience, and context to establish the purpose of texts.

verdicts.evidence: 'Why do you think the author wrote the book?' (Responses will vary, but may include: to imagine what the sun and moon might think about, and/or to describe the wonderful things that happen on earth at night.)
verdicts.rationale: The first clause is partially met: in Closing A, students engage in a Think-Pair-Share to answer "'Why do you think the author wrote the book?'" and generate responses about the author's purpose (e.g., "to imagine what the sun and moon might think about, and/or to describe the wonderful things that happen on earth at night"). This is the student discerning the purpose of a text being interpreted, but the activity addresses only the author dimension — audience and context are not developed or applied by students. The second clause (establish purpose of texts being constructed) is not met because students never set or articulate a purpose for a text they are constructing. The third clause (evaluate the extent to which texts achieve their purposes) is not met because no activity asks students to judge how well the text or their own writing achieves its purpose.

verdicts.evidence: 'What does it mean that moon wished for nothing more than to spend the rest of her nights?' (He didn't wish for anything else. He just wanted to spend time at night.)
verdicts.rationale: The standard requires students to determine meanings of unfamiliar words/concepts by applying context, academic vocabulary knowledge, and word parts. The Mini Language Dive in Work Time A partially addresses the context-clues clause: students work through chunked text to determine the meaning of "wished for nothing more than to spend the rest of his nights enjoying the exciting and wonderful things that came to life in his moonlight," with student responses such as "He didn't wish for anything else. He just wanted to spend time at night." This shows students using surrounding context to determine meaning. However, this activity is limited to ELLs and is a scaffolded sub-routine rather than the lesson's core instructional intent, capping the context clause at partially met. No activity has students apply knowledge of academic vocabulary to unlock unfamiliar words, and no activity has students use word parts (prefixes, suffixes, roots) to determine meaning — those clauses are not met.
